rooms.intro: In this room: a fake delivery text, a phishing email, and two real emails that are safe.
caseNotes: You have not ordered anything this month.
You reserved a book at Riverside Public Library on Monday.
You signed up for Saturday's park clean-up. Sam is the volunteer team's organiser.
lessons: Spot a fake delivery text: unexpected, rushed, a small fee and a strange link.
Name phishing and spot a fake look-alike address.
Recognise a real notice: it matches something you did, gives you time and asks for nothing secret.
Know that not every message is a scam: a real one from someone you know just shares details.

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 16: Information Security Best Practices (user awareness)
questions.explanation: You didn't order anything, so there is no package. The text comes from a random mobile number, rushes you with a 12-hour deadline, and links to a site that isn't the courier's. The small fee is bait to get your card or e-wallet details.
questions.feedback: Scam! No order + a small fee + a rush deadline = a fake delivery text. Don't tap the link.
questions.learningObjective: Spot a fake delivery text: unexpected, rushed, a small fee and a strange link.
questions.body: SwiftParcel: Your package is ON HOLD due to an incomplete address. Pay the ₱29 redelivery fee within 12 hours or it will be returned:
questions.scenarioContext: You have not ordered anything this month.
questions.hint: Compare the text with your case notes: were you expecting a package? Then check who sent it and where the link goes.

inspectables.label: Sender
inspectables.finding: An ordinary mobile number, not a named courier. Real delivery companies text from their own name or a short code.

inspectables.label: The claim
inspectables.finding: Your case notes say you haven't ordered anything this month - so which package?

inspectables.label: The request
inspectables.finding: A small fee is bait: the real goal is your card or e-wallet details.

inspectables.label: Deadline
inspectables.finding: A short deadline pushes you to act before you think.

inspectables.label: Link
inspectables.finding: swiftparcel-redeliver.example is not an official courier site, and it starts with http (not secure).

evidence.title: Ordinary mobile number
evidence.whyItMatters: Couriers don't text from random mobile numbers.

evidence.title: No order to deliver
evidence.whyItMatters: You haven't ordered anything, so there is no real package.

evidence.title: Asks for a payment
evidence.whyItMatters: Small fees are used to steal card and e-wallet details.

evidence.title: Pressure to act fast
evidence.whyItMatters: Scams rush you so you don't stop to check.

evidence.title: Unofficial, insecure link
evidence.whyItMatters: The link isn't the courier's site and isn't secure.

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Introduction to Computer Security: "types of security threats… in both personal and organizational contexts"
questions.explanation: Phishing is a fake message that tricks you into giving away your password. This one copies the school (uphs1 uses the number 1, not the letter l), scares you with a deadline and asks you to sign in. Real storage warnings never ask for your password.
questions.feedback: Phishing! Look closely: uphs1, not uphsl. Fake sender + scary deadline + "sign in here" = phishing.
questions.learningObjective: Name phishing and spot a fake look-alike address.
choices: Phishing
Ransomware
Denial-of-service attack
A normal storage warning
questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.body: Email from: Campus IT Helpdesk <helpdesk@uphs1-binan.example> Subject: Mailbox 98% full: verify now "Your school mailbox will be DELETED in 24 hours. Click below and sign in to verify your account." What kind of threat is this?
questions.hint: Check the sender's address letter by letter, then ask yourself what the email wants you to do.

inspectables.label: Sender address
inspectables.finding: Look closely: uphs1 uses the number 1 instead of the letter l. It's a lookalike of the school's real domain.

inspectables.label: Subject
inspectables.finding: Full mailboxes really happen. On its own this isn't a warning sign - look at what the email asks you to do.

inspectables.label: Threat
inspectables.finding: A scary deadline pushes you to act fast without checking.

inspectables.match: sign in to verify your account
inspectables.label: What it asks
inspectables.finding: It wants your password through a link. Real IT staff never ask you to 'verify' your password by email.

inspectables.label: The button
inspectables.finding: It leads to a sign-in page from an email link - the way fake pages collect passwords. (Simulated: nothing opens.)

evidence.title: Lookalike sender domain
evidence.whyItMatters: uphs1 is not uphsl - a fake address made to look real.

evidence.title: Scary deadline
evidence.whyItMatters: Threats and short deadlines are pressure tactics.

evidence.title: Asks you to sign in through a link
evidence.whyItMatters: That's how fake pages collect passwords.

questions.curriculumRef: Social and Professional Issues (BIT2105) — Week 15: Data Privacy Act (RA 10173)
questions.explanation: A raffle only needs a way to contact you, not your ID and birthdate. Together, those can be used to pretend to be you. The Data Privacy Act says they must explain why they collect data and take only what they need.
questions.feedback: Too much! An ID photo for a raffle? Ask why they need it and look for a privacy notice.
questions.learningObjective: Share personal data only when it's really needed and the reason is explained.
choices: They want a photo of your ID and your birthdate just to join, with no notice saying why
The raffle is free to join
The staff wear company shirts
The draw is next week
questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.body: A raffle booth at the mall asks you to fill in a form to join. Which of these is the biggest privacy warning sign?
questions.hint: Think about what a raffle really needs from you just to contact a winner.

inspectables.label: Full name
inspectables.finding: A raffle needs to know who won. Asking for a name is reasonable.

inspectables.label: Mobile number
inspectables.finding: A raffle needs a way to contact the winner. This is proportionate.

inspectables.label: Birthdate
inspectables.finding: A raffle doesn't need your birthdate. Together with an ID photo it can be used for identity theft.

inspectables.label: ID photo
inspectables.finding: Far more than joining a raffle needs. An ID photo is valuable to identity thieves.

inspectables.label: Privacy notice
inspectables.finding: Without a notice you can't know why your data is collected or what happens to it (transparency).

inspectables.label: Free entry
inspectables.finding: Free raffles are normal. Not a warning sign on its own.

inspectables.label: Staff
inspectables.finding: Uniforms are easy to copy and prove little either way. Not a warning sign on its own.

evidence.title: Asks for an ID photo
evidence.whyItMatters: Collect only what is needed (proportionality).

evidence.title: Asks for your birthdate
evidence.whyItMatters: Birthdates help thieves pretend to be you.

evidence.title: No privacy notice
evidence.whyItMatters: People must be told why their data is collected (transparency).

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 9: Information Assets and Asset Management ("evaluate their value and protection requirements")
questions.explanation: "Forgot password" links go to your email. Whoever controls your email can reset your other accounts: social media, e-wallets and school. Protect it first with a unique password and MFA (a second check, like a code).
questions.feedback: Your email is the master key. Every "Forgot password" link goes there.
questions.learningObjective: Protect first the account that unlocks all the others.
choices: Your online game account
Your main email account, which receives password-reset links
Your music streaming account
An old forum account you no longer use
questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.body: A scammer who gets into one account may use it to get into your others. Which account needs the strongest protection?
questions.hint: Where do "Forgot password" links get sent?

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Operating System Security ("patch management, and security configuration")
questions.explanation: This is a tech-support scam. Real warnings come from your computer's own security app, not from a web page with a phone number. The "support" person will ask for money or control of your PC. Close the tab. If it's stuck, close the browser with Task Manager.
questions.feedback: Scam! Real alerts come from your computer's settings, never from a web page that tells you to call.
questions.learningObjective: Know where real security alerts come from.
questions.subject: SYSTEM SECURITY ALERT
questions.body: Your computer is INFECTED and LOCKED. Call Certified Support at 1-800-555-0199 now. DO NOT restart your computer.
questions.scenarioContext: While browsing, a full-screen red page appeared and started beeping.
questions.hint: Where do real security warnings come from: a web page, or your own computer?

inspectables.label: The page
inspectables.finding: A page you didn't ask for, from a site you don't know.

inspectables.label: The alert
inspectables.finding: Big red alerts are designed to cause panic.

inspectables.label: The claim
inspectables.finding: A web page can't scan your computer. It's only a page made to scare you.

inspectables.label: What it wants
inspectables.finding: Real security warnings never ask you to call a number. This is a tech-support scam.

inspectables.label: The instruction
inspectables.finding: It keeps you on the scary page. Closing the browser usually ends it.

evidence.title: Fake infection claim
evidence.whyItMatters: Web pages can't see what's on your computer.

evidence.title: Asks you to call 'support'
evidence.whyItMatters: Real warnings don't come with a phone number.

evidence.title: Keeps you from closing it
evidence.whyItMatters: Pressure is the scam's main tool.

questions.curriculumRef: Cyber Forensics (BIT2226) — Digital Evidence and Evidence Collection ("collection, preservation, and documentation")
questions.explanation: Proof is what lets PayLite and the police help you, and the reference number can help trace the money. Deleting the chat destroys proof. Public threats can get you in trouble. "Pay more to get a refund" is a second scam.
questions.feedback: Save the proof first: chat, profile and reference number. Then report it.
questions.learningObjective: Save proof before doing anything else.
choices: Delete the chat so you can move on
Post the seller's photo and threaten them publicly
Send another payment because they say it "unlocks" your refund
Save proof (the chat, the seller's profile and the receipt with its reference number), then report to PayLite and the police
questions.subject: What Should You Do?
questions.body: You paid ₱1,500 to an online seller through PayLite. The seller then blocked you and never shipped. What should you do first?
questions.hint: After a scam, what will the e-wallet company and the police ask you to show them?

inspectables.label: Your chat
inspectables.finding: The chat shows what was agreed and paid. Keep it - it's evidence.

inspectables.label: Blocked
inspectables.finding: Being blocked after paying is a classic sign of a fake seller. Save everything before it disappears.

inspectables.label: Payment receipt
inspectables.finding: The reference number lets PayLite trace where the money went.

inspectables.label: Seller's profile
inspectables.finding: The seller's account details help the platform and the police find them.

evidence.title: The chat history
evidence.whyItMatters: Proof of what was agreed. Deleting it destroys evidence.

evidence.title: Receipt with reference number
evidence.whyItMatters: Reference numbers can help trace the money.

evidence.title: Seller's account details
evidence.whyItMatters: They let the platform and the police act.

inspectables.finding: no-reply@novacloud.example matches the trusted domain in your case files.

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Web and Application Security
questions.explanation: To find the real website, read the address from right to left, up to the first single "/". Here it is account-verify.example. The "examplebank" in front is a decoy the scammer added. Nothing is misspelled, and HTTPS doesn't make it safe.
questions.feedback: Read right to left: the real site is account-verify.example. The bank's name is just a decoy.
questions.learningObjective: Find the real website in a link by reading right to left.
choices: It's ExampleBank's site because "examplebank" appears first
It's safe because it uses HTTPS
It's a subdomain trick: the real domain is account-verify.example
It's a misspelled (typosquatted) bank domain
questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.body: A message links to: https://examplebank.example.account-verify.example/login. Which is true?
questions.hint: Read the web address from right to left, up to the first single slash.

inspectables.label: https://
inspectables.finding: HTTPS only encrypts the connection. It doesn't tell you who owns the site.

inspectables.label: The left part
inspectables.finding: Everything to the left of the real domain is a subdomain - the attacker can write anything there, even a bank's name.

inspectables.label: The real domain
inspectables.finding: Read the domain from the right, ending just before the first single '/'. The real domain is account-verify.example.

inspectables.label: The path
inspectables.finding: The part after the '/' can say anything. It doesn't change who owns the site.

inspectables.label: The page
inspectables.finding: Copying a bank's look is easy. Nothing is misspelled here, so this isn't typosquatting either.

evidence.title: Real domain: account-verify.example
evidence.whyItMatters: The domain decides who owns the page.

evidence.title: Bank name used as a subdomain
evidence.whyItMatters: Subdomain tricks put a trusted name on the left.

rooms.intro: In this room: what the padlock means, impostors asking for money, owning up to a mistake, second login checks, fake Wi-Fi and fake bank texts.
lessons: Know that a padlock doesn't mean a site is real.
Spot scams that use feelings and rush you, and check through a number you know.
Report a security mistake quickly and honestly.
Pick the protection that fits the problem.
Spot fake Wi-Fi hotspots, and know what a VPN can't do.
Know that the name on your phone doesn't prove who sent a text.

questions.curriculumRef: Advanced Cybersecurity Strategies (BIT4233). Supporting: Computer Security (BIT1225), Cryptography — Modern Cryptography ("secure data in transit and at rest")
questions.explanation: The padlock (HTTPS) means your connection is private, so others can't read what you send. It doesn't say who owns the site. Anyone can get a padlock, scam sites too, so you still need to check the address.
questions.feedback: Padlock = private connection, not safe site. Fake sites have padlocks too.
questions.learningObjective: Know that a padlock doesn't mean a site is real.
choices: The site is owned by the real company
Data between you and this site is encrypted, but the site itself could still be fake
The site has been checked by the government
The site cannot contain malware
questions.subject: Multiple Choice
questions.body: A login page shows a padlock and starts with https://. What does the padlock actually prove?
questions.hint: A padlock is about the connection. Does it tell you who owns the site?

inspectables.label: https://
inspectables.finding: The 's' means the connection uses TLS encryption. Others on the network can't read or change your data.

inspectables.label: The padlock
inspectables.finding: The connection is private - data in transit is encrypted. It says nothing about who runs the site.

inspectables.label: The certificate
inspectables.finding: Certificates are easy for anyone to get for their own domain - scam sites have padlocks too.

inspectables.label: The form
inspectables.finding: A padlock doesn't make a form safe to fill in. You still have to check the domain.

evidence.title: Encrypted connection
evidence.whyItMatters: That's what the padlock actually means.

evidence.title: Anyone can get a certificate
evidence.whyItMatters: So a padlock can't prove the site is the real company.

items.text: https://login-page.example/signin

items.label: click to view
items.text: Padlock: Connection is secure

questions.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Weeks 10–11: Cybersecurity Threats and Attack Landscape
questions.explanation: A "family member" with a new number, a sudden emergency, a money request and "don't call me" are classic signs. This trick is called social engineering: it uses your feelings, not hacking. Call Migs's old number, or ask something only he would know.
questions.feedback: Impersonation! New number + emergency + "don't call" = call the old number first.
questions.learningObjective: Spot scams that use feelings and rush you, and check through a number you know.
choices: Impersonation: someone pretending to be family with a "new number"
Malware infection
A data breach
A promotional spam message
questions.subject: Identify the Threat
questions.body: SMS from an unknown number: "Ma, si Migs 'to. Nasira phone ko, bagong number ko 'to. Pa-send naman ₱3,000 sa PayLite 0917 555 0188, emergency lang. Wag ka muna tumawag, wala pa akong load." What attack is this? In English: "Mom, it's Migs. My phone broke, this is my new number. Please send ₱3,000 to PayLite 0917 555 0188, it's an emergency. Don't call yet, I have no load."
questions.hint: A new number, an emergency, a money request and "don't call me". How could you check it's really him?

inspectables.label: Sender
inspectables.finding: Not in your contacts. The first text explains it away with a 'new number'.

inspectables.label: "New number"
inspectables.finding: Claiming to be family on a new number is how impersonators skip your contacts list.

inspectables.label: The request
inspectables.finding: The whole story leads to one thing: send money now.

inspectables.label: Emergency
inspectables.finding: An invented emergency rushes you past checking.

inspectables.label: "Don't call yet"
inspectables.finding: It stops you from calling Migs's old number - the easiest way to check.

evidence.title: Claims to be family on a new number
evidence.whyItMatters: Impersonation exploits trust, not technology.

evidence.title: Asks for money
evidence.whyItMatters: The goal of the story.

evidence.title: Invented emergency
evidence.whyItMatters: Urgency stops you from thinking.

evidence.title: Blocks you from checking
evidence.whyItMatters: Call the old number or ask something only Migs would know.

questions.curriculumRef: Social and Professional Issues (BIT2105). Supporting: IAS Week 16 (incident reporting procedures) — Weeks 13–14: Security Incidents ("recommend appropriate preventive and corrective measures")
questions.explanation: Act fast. Changing your password makes the stolen one useless, and IT can block the fake site and warn others. Hiding it gives the attacker time. Forwarding spreads the bad link, and deleting removes the proof IT needs.
questions.feedback: Report it! Mistakes happen. Hiding them is what makes them worse.
questions.learningObjective: Report a security mistake quickly and honestly.
choices: Say nothing, since nothing bad has happened yet
Forward the email to coworkers to ask if they got it too
Delete the email so no one finds out
Change your password on the official site now, report it to IT, and watch for sign-ins you didn't make
questions.subject: What Should You Do?
questions.body: During your OJT, you typed your work password into a page you opened from an email. A minute later, you notice the address was wrong.
questions.hint: If your password may be stolen, what makes the stolen one useless, and who needs to know?

inspectables.label: The real domain
inspectables.finding: Read from the right: the real domain is login-verify.example - not your company's. This was a fake page.

inspectables.label: The message
inspectables.finding: Fake pages often say 'verified' so you don't worry. Nothing was verified - your password was collected.

inspectables.label: What you typed
inspectables.finding: The attacker now has your work password. Every minute counts.

inspectables.match: The email that sent you to this page
inspectables.label: The email
inspectables.finding: IT needs this email to block the site and warn others. Don't delete it or forward it to coworkers.

evidence.title: It was a fake page
evidence.whyItMatters: The domain wasn't your company's.

evidence.title: Your password is stolen

questions.feedback: Check by phone, on a number you already have. A real account can still be used by a scammer.
questions.learningObjective: Double-check risky requests another way, even from trusted accounts.
choices: Pay it, since the email passed authentication and came from the real address
Reply to the email asking the director to confirm
Pay half now and half after confirming
Call the director and the supplier on numbers you already have before changing any bank details

inspectables.label: "Don't call"

questions.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Incident Response and Forensics
questions.explanation: First, stop it spreading: cut the network so it can't reach other PCs. Leave the PC on so investigators keep the evidence. Paying doesn't promise your files back, restarting can erase evidence, and a USB can carry the infection.
questions.feedback: Disconnect, keep it on, report. Stop the spread first. Investigators need the evidence.
questions.learningObjective: Know the first steps: stop the spread, keep the evidence, report.
choices: Pay quickly before the price goes up
Unplug it from the network (or turn off Wi-Fi), leave it on, stop using it, and report to IT right away
Restart, run a cleanup tool and delete the ransom note
Copy your files to your USB drive to save them

questions.body: After you open an email attachment on a lab PC, your files start changing to .locked and a note demands cryptocurrency. What do you do first?

inspectables.label: Network

inspectables.label: Power

questions.explanation: Using stolen passwords, even to help, is not allowed and can hurt the victims more. Posting the link sends more people to the fake page, and testing it gives away your own password. Report it: IT has the right to act. Post the link on the freedom wall to warn everyone
Test it with your own real password to confirm it works
Report it to the school's IT office with screenshots and the web address, without logging in or using the stolen data

reserve.curriculumRef: Information Assurance in Security 1 (BIT1101) — Week 3: Fundamentals of Information Security (CIA Triad)
reserve.explanation: Confidentiality means keeping information private. A stranger can now read Ana's grades and messages, so her privacy is broken. Integrity would mean her data was changed. Availability would mean she was locked out.
reserve.feedback: Confidentiality! Ana's info wasn't changed or locked. It was seen by someone who shouldn't see it.
reserve.learningObjective: Name the security goal that a scam breaks.
choices: Availability
Integrity
Confidentiality
None, because she typed it in herself
reserve.subject: Multiple Choice
reserve.body: Ana typed her student login into a fake "school portal" page. The scammer can now read her grades, messages and personal details. Which security goal was broken? CIA Triad: Confidentiality = kept private · Integrity = kept unchanged · Availability = ready to use
reserve.hint: Think about what happened to Ana's information: was it changed, locked away, or seen by someone who shouldn't see it?

inspectables.label: The page
inspectables.finding: It only looks like the school portal. Whatever Ana typed went straight to the scammer.

inspectables.match: read her grades, messages and personal details
inspectables.label: What the scammer can do
inspectables.finding: The scammer can now look at Ana's private information. Was anything changed or locked - or only seen?

evidence.title: Fake login page
evidence.whyItMatters: Fake pages copy real ones to collect what you type.

evidence.title: Private details exposed
evidence.whyItMatters: Someone who isn't allowed can now read Ana's information.

reserve.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Authentication and Access Control
reserve.explanation: A one-time code (OTP) is like a key: whoever has it can approve payments as you. A real bank never asks you to read it out. Hang up and call the number on your card, a number you already trust.
reserve.feedback: Hang up! No real bank asks for your OTP. Call back on the number on your card.
reserve.learningObjective: Never share an OTP, and call back on a number you trust.
choices: Read the code quickly to stop the fraud
Give only the first three digits
Ask them to email you instead
Hang up and call the number on the back of your card or in the official app
reserve.subject: What Should You Do?
reserve.body: A caller says: "This is ExampleBank's fraud department. Someone is using your card right now. We just sent you a 6-digit code. Read it to me so we can block the transaction."
reserve.hint: Who should ever see your one-time code? And how could you check that the caller is really your bank?

inspectables.label: Who they say they are
inspectables.finding: Anyone can claim to be your bank on the phone. You didn't call them - they called you.

inspectables.label: Pressure
inspectables.finding: Creating panic stops you from thinking clearly.

inspectables.label: The request
inspectables.finding: That code is your one-time password (OTP). Whoever has it can approve logins and payments as you.

inspectables.label: The code you received
inspectables.finding: A one-time code proves that YOU are approving something. A real bank never asks you to read it aloud.

evidence.title: Unverified caller
evidence.whyItMatters: A caller's name or claim proves nothing.

evidence.title: Panic and urgency
evidence.whyItMatters: Urgency is used to stop you from checking.

evidence.title: Asks for your OTP
evidence.whyItMatters: No real bank ever asks you to read out a one-time code.

reserve.curriculumRef: Computer Security (BIT1225) — Malware and Threats: "preventing, detecting, and removing malware, including… anti-malware tools"
reserve.explanation: A safe program never needs your antivirus turned off. Fake "free skins" tools often hide malware that steals your saved passwords. Scanning afterwards is too late, and sending it to a friend puts them at risk.
reserve.feedback: Don't run it! When someone asks you to turn off your antivirus, they want to get past it.
reserve.learningObjective: Treat any request to turn off security tools as a warning sign.
choices: Turn off the antivirus just for a minute and run it
Run it, then scan your PC afterwards
Don't download it, and block or report the sender
Send it to a friend to test first

inspectables.finding: You don't know this person, and the offer came out of nowhere.

inspectables.label: The file

inspectables.label: The request
